title: China Import Watch
dek: China's crude buying: import volumes, sourcing shifts, teapot run rates, and what it means for sour barrel demand.

claims.text: Goldman Sachs estimated China's seaborne crude net imports rose about 6 percent in September from August but stayed almost 3 million barrels per day below normal seasonal levels, and its models point to only about 600,000 barrels per day more total crude imports in the fourth quarter versus the third. The bank estimates a sustained 1 million barrel per day change in China's net crude imports over six months would shift Brent's fair value by about 4 dollars a barrel.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell's analysis of official data (published Sep 15, 2026) showed China processed 13.91 million b/d in August, the most since March, against 8.93 million b/d of imports plus 4.34 million b/d of domestic production, implying a 640,000 b/d inventory draw. It was the third draw in four months (draws of 500,000 b/d in May and 940,000 b/d in June, a 210,000 b/d surplus in July); stocks are estimated at at least 1.2 billion barrels, and January to August still showed a net surplus of 330,000 b/d.

Kpler data cited by Maritime Professional (Sep 23, 2026) put Asia on course to import 23.96 million b/d of crude in September, up from 23.38 million in August and the highest since February, extending the recovery from April's decade-plus low. Even so, September remained 13% below the 27.55 million b/d three-month pre-conflict average through February.
claims.vintage: Prelim data: Sep 2026; published Sep 23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

claims.text: Russian and Iranian crude accounted for less than one-third of China's September imports, down from about half in August, as China shifted toward non-sanctioned supply, per Goldman Sachs analysis. The bank said the shift toward openly traded crude could make changes in Chinese purchasing more visible in benchmark pricing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview on Sep 27 that only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade, with final deliveries to China expected within about two weeks, after which he claimed Iran would have nothing left to trade. That is an unverified prediction from the official directing the sanctions effort, not independent evidence that Iranian exports have stopped.

TankerTrackers reported Sep 24 that almost 6 million barrels of confiscated Iranian crude, including the 1.88-million-barrel tanker Majestic X seized in the Indian Ocean in April while headed for China, were crossing the Atlantic toward the United States. The report relies on a single tracking source and should be treated as a lead until corroborated.
claims.vintage: TankerTrackers report Sep 24, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: Saudi Aramco cut its September official selling price (OSP) for Arab Light to Asia by 50 cents a barrel to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark, the fifth-lowest differential since 2000, per Energies Media (Aug 19, 2026). The cut reflected war-driven costs (freight, rerouting) plus formal discount requests from Asian refiners for longer voyages; Aramco held exports near 5 million b/d, about 70% of normal, leaning on Red Sea port Yanbu and potentially Sidi Kerir loadings.

Saudi Arabia left its October-loading Arab Light official selling price (OSP) to Asia unchanged, according to Reuters reporting via TradingView on Sep 3, 2026, pausing the easing that had taken the September price to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark.

Gasoline inventories at state-owned majors fell 2.9 percent in a week to their lowest since 2022 and diesel stocks hit a 15-month low after a 2.4 percent drop, per commodity research firm JLC International cited by Bloomberg. Energy Aspects analyst Jiana Sun told Bloomberg there is a growing risk Beijing caps monthly clean product exports at about 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter.

Energy News Beat (Sep 13, 2026) reported the second batch of 2026 clean-product export quotas brought China's total 2026 allocation to about 32 million tonnes. August product exports hit 6.01 million tonnes, up 12.7% year on year, but January to August exports were still down 9.6% year on year, with gasoline down 57% year to date, consistent with a policy-managed surplus rather than an unconstrained export boom.

General Administration of Customs (GAC) data reported by IDNFinancials (Sep 18, 2026) gave August per-fuel detail: gasoline exports 700,000 tonnes, down 17.5% year on year but the highest since October 2025; diesel 1.33 million tonnes, up 42.1% year on year and the highest since March 2024; jet fuel a record 2.55 million tonnes, up 41.4% year on year. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports fell 17.8% year on year to 5.16 million tonnes.

Baird Maritime (Sep 21, 2026, citing GAC customs data) reported China's August fuel oil exports fell to 1.21 million tonnes (about 247,000 b/d), down 35% month on month and 27% year on year, the lowest since October 2024, partly on weather disruption at the Zhoushan bunkering hub. Fuel oil imports were 1.3 million tonnes, up 15% month on month and down 11% year on year; crude throughput climbed for a second month, supported by stronger fuel exports after Beijing eased export restrictions in mid-July.

Baltic Exchange data put the time charter equivalent for a 270,000-ton very large crude carrier (VLCC) on the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China route at about 1.212 million dollars per day on Sep 17, up from about 1.034 million the day before and roughly 700,000 at the start of September. The Baltic's Sep 18 weekly report put TD3C at Worldscale 1,140, the Gulf of Oman to China TD34 route at 870,947 dollars per day, and West Africa to China TD15 at 524,575 dollars per day.

The 2016-built VLCC Kuwait Prosperity, operated by Sinokor, was fixed at Worldscale 1,350 for a Persian Gulf to east voyage loading by Total Singapore on Sep 22, with a daily equivalent estimated above 1 million dollars. Analysts attribute the spike to reduced Hormuz transits, longer voyages via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and diversions around the Cape of Good Hope adding an estimated 11 to 14 million dollars per voyage in charter costs alone.
claims.vintage: Fixture for Sep 22 loading; reported Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: Tide Signal News (Sep 23, 2026, citing Reuters/Baltic Exchange data) reported very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight from the Gulf of Oman to China hit Worldscale 450, about $11.50 per barrel, a record for the route and up roughly 65% from the Sep 4 TD34 assessment, as conflict risk shrank the pool of tankers willing to trade around the Gulf.

Vessel Hunter News (Sep 22, 2026, citing Baltic Exchange data) reported the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China very large crude carrier (VLCC) time-charter equivalent reached $1.2125 million a day on Sep 17, up 40.6% on the week and roughly ten times the $117,400 a day before the February conflict. TD15 West Africa to Far East hit $524,500 a day and TD22 US Gulf to Far East $388,400 a day; the China Crude Oil Tanker Freight Index stood at 14,575 points on Sep 16, about 83% above its early-September level.
claims.source: Vessel Hunter News (citing Baltic Exchange data)

claims.text: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air's August 2026 snapshot (published Sep 17, 2026) found refinery throughput down 6.9% year on year in August, though recovered from July's slump. New energy vehicle (NEV) output rose 21.9% year on year to 61% of all vehicles produced, and battery production surged 70% year on year, consistent with continued structural gasoline displacement.
claims.source: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

claims.text: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), in analysis published April 2026, classifies China's strategic oil inventories at an estimated 1.397 billion barrels, comprising about 360 million barrels government-held and 1 billion barrels commercial. The EIA treats both as strategic because China's national oil companies have reportedly been instructed since 2024 to hold emergency oil in commercial tanks.

Geospatial firm Kayrros, via MEXC reporting from the Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC) in Singapore, estimated China's strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) at about 415 million barrels and commercial stocks at about 780 million barrels in early September 2026, up close to 130 million barrels combined since late March, with above-ground capacity use near 60.5%, leaving room for further builds.
claims.vintage: Estimate: early Sep 2026; reported from APPEC; accessed 2026-09-24
claims.source: MEXC (citing Kayrros chief analyst Antoine Halff at APPEC)
